extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements amount to an "inventive concept" (i.e., are "significantly more" than a judicial exception) under the Alice/Mayo framework during USPTO examination. Focuses on identifying additional elements, analyzing them individually and in combination, and assessing improvements to computer or other technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Do additional elements amount to an inventive concept?
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer by first identifying whether any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) are recited beyond the judicial exception(s), then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept (i.e., amount to significantly more than the judicial exception(s)). Use the Supreme Court considerations introduced in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(h). This evaluation is not a weighing test — it is important to evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the applicant’s invention and whether the additional elements encompass an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry over findings from Step 2A Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should carry over identification of the additional element(s) in the claim from Step 2A Prong Two and carry over conclusions from Step 2A Prong Two on considerations discussed in MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(c),(e),(f),(h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-evaluate any additional element or combination previously considered to be 'insignificant extra-solution activity' under MPEP § 2106.05(g), because a new finding that an element is unconventional or more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity may change the Step 2B determination. Also evaluate whether elements are other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity or simply append such activities at a high level of generality per MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome determination at Step 2B (Pathway C or rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim as a whole does not amount to significantly more than the exception itself (no inventive concept), the claim is not eligible (Step 2B: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101; if the claim as a whole does amount to significantly more than the exception (there is an inventive concept), the claim is eligible (Step 2B: YES) at Pathway C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2B concludes the eligibility analysis. Use the flowchart in MPEP § 2106, subsection III to determine whether to issue an ineligibility rejection (see MPEP § 2106.07 for formulating 35 U.S.C. 101 rejections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine each claim separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application. One claim may be ineligible while another dependent claim may be eligible because it recites additional elements that amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether the claim improves computer functioning or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining patent eligibility, examiners should consider whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration is the search for a technological solution to a technological problem. It should be evaluated at Step 2A Prong Two and at Step 2B (and in streamlined analysis where appropriate). Relevant precedents include Alice, DDR Holdings, Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, Amdocs, and others. Improvements may support finding an inventive concept; mere use of a computer as a tool typically does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must provide a technical explanation of the asserted improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is asserted that the invention improves upon conventional functioning of a computer or other technology, a technical explanation as to how to implement the invention should be present in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must provide sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill in the art would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. The specification need not explicitly recite the improvement, but the improvement must be apparent to a person of ordinary skill. Conclusory assertions of improvement without necessary detail are insufficient (see McRO v. Affinity Labs contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the disclosed improvement; evaluate claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: After the examiner has determined the specification discloses an improvement, the claim must be evaluated to ensure the claim itself reflects the disclosed improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim must include components or steps that provide the improvement described in the specification. The claim does not need to recite the improvement in 'thereby' language; the full scope under the broadest reasonable interpretation should be considered. Evaluate the claim 'as an ordered combination' and avoid oversimplifying the claims by ignoring specific requirements of individual steps (see Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement can be provided by additional elements alone or combined with the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial exception alone cannot provide the improvement; the improvement can be provided by one or more additional elements or by additional elements in combination with the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the claim as a whole to determine whether the additional elements (alone or in combination with the exception) supply the inventive concept (references: Diamond v. Diehr; Finjan v. Blue Coat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement consideration applies across technologies but not to abstract-idea improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The consideration of improvements is relevant regardless of the technology of the claimed invention (computer-implemented, life sciences, or other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improvement in technology (e.g., new way to preserve hepatocytes) can demonstrate eligibility. However, an improvement in the abstract idea itself (e.g., a better economic practice) is not an improvement in technology (see Trading Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true computer-functionality improvements from mere use of computers
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-related technologies, determine whether the claim purports to improve computer capabilities or instead invokes computers merely as a tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed invention provides a specific implementation or technical solution (e.g., data structure, distributed architecture, particular server structure) rather than generic post-hoc recitation of computers. Relevant cases and example categories that courts have found may show improvement include Enfish, DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Research Corp. Techs., Amdocs v. Openet, Visual Memory v. NVIDIA, TLI Communications, Apple v. Ameranth, Finjan, Core Wireless, Data Engine Techs., Ancora Tech. The examiner should assess whether the claim covers a particular solution to a problem rather than merely the idea of a solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that may not show improvement in computer-functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain claim characteristics the courts have indicated may be insufficient to show improvement in computer-functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (i) generating menus with functionally claimed features (Ameranth); (ii) accelerating processing only by relying on general-purpose computer speed (FairWarning); (iii) mere automation of manual processes using a generic computer (Credit Acceptance; LendingTree non-precedential); (iv) recording/transmitting/archiving digital images using conventional tech without technical detail (TLI Communications); (v) affixing a barcode without technical details of generation/processing (Secured Mail Solutions); (vi) mere instructions to display two sets of information without how to achieve it (Interval Licensing); (vii) improving information stored by a database without improving database functionality (BSG Tech v. BuySeasons); (viii) arranging GUI information to assist traders without technical improvement (Trading Technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims must require computer implementation to show computer improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation; a claim whose entire scope can be performed mentally cannot be said to improve computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed process can be practiced verbally or mentally, or all steps can be performed mentally by a skilled artisan, it does not improve computer technology (see Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics; RecogniCorp v. Nintendo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant burden to rebut examiner on improvement using 37 CFR 1.132 evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner concludes the disclosed invention does not improve technology, the burden shifts to the applicant to provide persuasive arguments supported by necessary evidence (e.g., declaration) under 37 CFR 1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any such evidence must establish what the specification would convey to one of ordinary skill in the art and cannot be used to supplement the specification. The examiner generally is not expected to make a qualitative judgment on the merits of the asserted improvement without such persuasive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-evaluate elements characterized as 'insignificant extra-solution activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-evaluate any additional element or combination of elements that was considered to be insignificant extra-solution activity per MPEP § 2106.05(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If re-evaluation finds the element is unconventional or otherwise more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity, this finding may indicate that the additional element is no longer insignificant and may supply an inventive concept under Step 2B.
